flashcards.q: What are the five steps of Johnson's algorithm?
flashcards.a: 1. Add virtual source with 0-weight edges to every vertex. 2. One Bellman-Ford pass from it for potentials h(v). 3. Check negative cycle. 4. Reweight w'(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(u)-h(v). 5. Dijkstra from every vertex, then convert dist(u,v)=dist'(u,v)-h(u)+h(v).

flashcards.q: Why is the reweighted edge weight w'(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(u)-h(v) always >= 0 (given no negative cycle)?
flashcards.a: Because Bellman-Ford's convergence guarantees h(v) <= h(u)+w(u,v) for every edge -- rearranging gives w(u,v)+h(u)-h(v) >= 0.

flashcards.q: Why does reweighting preserve which path is shortest between two fixed vertices?
flashcards.a: Summing the reweighted cost over any path from u to v telescopes to the real cost plus h(u)-h(v), a constant added to every path between the same two endpoints -- so relative ordering of paths is unaffected.

flashcards.q: What is Johnson's algorithm's total complexity and how does it compare to Floyd-Warshall on a sparse graph?
flashcards.a: O(VE + V^2 log V) vs Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3). At V=10,000, E=30,000: Johnson's ~1.3*10^9 operations vs Floyd-Warshall's ~10^12 -- three orders of magnitude difference.

flashcards.q: Why must the virtual source's edges point TO every vertex, not from every vertex to it?
flashcards.a: So Bellman-Ford can compute a well-defined potential h(v) for every vertex in one hop; edges in the wrong direction leave potentials undefined or introduce a spurious cycle through the virtual source.

flashcards.q: When is Johnson's algorithm NOT worth using over Floyd-Warshall?
flashcards.a: On dense graphs (E ~ V^2), where Johnson's O(VE+V^2 log V) approaches the same cubic order as Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) but with much more implementation complexity for no real gain.

flashcards.q: What happens if you skip the negative-cycle check in Johnson's algorithm?
flashcards.a: Shortest paths are undefined with a negative cycle present; the potentials won't have actually converged, so reweighted edges aren't guaranteed non-negative, and Dijkstra silently produces wrong distances with no error.

flashcards.q: For repeated point-to-point shortest path queries at massive scale (500k+ nodes), what beats materializing Johnson's O(V^2) all-pairs matrix?
flashcards.a: Contraction hierarchies or hub labeling -- heavier one-time preprocessing that answers individual queries near-instantly without ever storing the full distance matrix.
